h: A penance in stone and a school in the abbey
p: Why is there an abbey on a battlefield at all? The story goes that William founded it as an act of penance for all the bloodshed of the Conquest, with the high altar placed on the spot where Harold was said to have fallen. Benedictine monks lived and worked here for centuries.

Then Henry VIII's Dissolution of the Monasteries brought it all to an end. The abbey was handed to Sir Anthony Browne, who turned parts of it into a grand house, and a big chunk of those buildings is now home to a school. That's why some areas you can see from the grounds aren't open to visitors: the pupils are using them.

Allow at least two to three hours, more if you want the full battlefield walk and a proper look round the ruins. English Heritage has often staged a big re-enactment around the anniversary weekend in October, so if you're a fan of clanging shields, keep an eye out for event dates.

The rest of 1066 Country is right on the doorstep. Pevensey Castle is near where William landed, Hastings has its old town, its fishing beach and the ruins of the castle William built, and the National Trust's Bodiam Castle, with its fairy-tale moat, is a short drive inland. Keen walkers can even follow the long-distance 1066 Country Walk, which passes through Battle on its way between Pevensey and Rye.
